newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - U.S. drug companies to post banner Q4.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - U.S. drug companies to post banner Q4.

text.p: U.S. drug companies are set to report their best quarter of 1996, with their fourth quarter earnings propelled by unit volume growth, a firm pricing environment and a wave of new drug approvals.
"The companies should do extremely well in the fourth quarter," Jack Lamberton, an analyst at NatWest Securties Corp, said. "The factors which are driving growth have been in evidence all year."
Fourth quarter earnings could be up anywhere from 17 to 22 percent for the core group of pharmaceutical companies, including Merck and Co Inc, Warner-Lambert Co and Eli Lilly and Co, analysts said.
Behind the jump was an accelerating pace of U.S. Food and Drug Administration product approvals, which brought more high-margin drugs to large target markets, analysts said.

"The FDA approved 58 new compounds in 1996, which is two times its average rate," James Keeney, an analyst at Rodman & Renshaw, said. "In 1995 it approved 30 new compounds, so there is a total of 88 new drugs out there."

Many of these new products have unique attributes, are aimed at new or large therapeutic markets, and have quickly become profitable for the industry once the introductory spending ended, Rodman and Renshaw said in a research note.
"Most companies have entered a new product breakout cycle virtually assuring high growth for several years," David Saks, an analyst at Gruntal and Co, said in a note.
Lilly is seen benefitting from sales of its newly-approved schizophrenia drug Zyprexa and Merck from strong sales of eight new prescription drugs launched in the past 18 months, Keeney said.
"We expect it to be the best quarter of the year for the pharmaceutical companies," Scott Shevick, an analyst at Bear Stearns, said. "Earnings should all be up double-digits."
Pricing has improved all year and strong cash flow has let companies pursue aggressive share buyback programs, he said.

Strong fundamentals are offsetting periodic problems overseas, like foreign exchange fluctuations, analysts said. Lamberton said foreign exchange could knock one or two percent off results. Others said the firm British pound was a cloud.
But Keeney said managed healthcare companies are prescribing more name-brand drugs rather than the cheaper generic equivalents, driving up prescription sales.

"The managed care companies are moving away from the least expensive product, partly to guarantee patient compliance," he said. While newer drugs are more expensive, they often have fewer unpleasant side effects, he said.
Lamberton also said drug companies are also not discounting as much to the managed care providers.
Cost cutting and corporate downsizing at the major U.S. drugmakers is also helping the bottom line, analysts said.
